To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

bilateral lesions of the rat retrosplenial cortex impair the ability of rabbits to learn a discrimination reversal task, a finding that is highly similar to the effects of bilateral hippocampectomies on reversal learning.

lesions of the retrosplential cortex result in severe impairments in reversal learning that parallel those seen after bilateral hippocamectomy, and that these deficits are highly similar to deficits observed after lesions of the cerebellar cortex.

Bilateral lesions of the retrosplential cortex produce deficits in discrimination reversal learning of rabbit eyeblink conditioning that are similar to those observed in rabbits with bilateral hippocampectomies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the cerebellum and its associated structures, particularly the hippocampus, in the control of conditioned responses.
elucidating the role that hippocampal-cerebellar interactions might play in the behavioral expression of the effects of hippocampal learning-related changes in pyramidal cell discharge.
elucidation of the role of the cerebellar cortex and cerebellar nuclei in the acquisition and expression of learned responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

lesions of the hippocampus, the retrosplenial and the cerebellar cortex produce similar deficits in the reversal of the rabbit n.m.r. and that the retrosplenial lesion is a good model to study the cerebellar deficit.

the retrosplenial lesion produced deficits in reversal learning which are highly similar to the deficits produced by hippocampectomy, and that these deficits are most likely due to the loss of the hippocampal projections to the cerebellar cortex.

the retrosplenial lesions produce a deficit in reversal learning of conditioned responding that is highly similar to that produced by hippocampectomy, and that the deficit in reversal learning produced by hippocampal lesions is not due to damage to the retrosphenial cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lesions of the retrosplenal cortex produce deficits in the acquisition of new memories that are similar to those observed following hippocampectomy.
the hippocampal formation is necessary for the expression of cerebellar learning.
the cerebellum is involved in the expression of hippocampal learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the retrosplenial region of the medial dorsal thalamus, which is the major target of hippocampal efferents and a critical link in the hippocampal-prefrontal-cerebellar circuit, is a key structure in the expression of hippocampus-dependent learning.
the retrosplenial and hippocampal brain areas may play a similar role in the acquisition of a new learning set, and that the hippocampus may play a more critical role in the reversal of that set.
the cerebellar cortex is a likely target for learning-related changes in the activity of hippocampal pyramids.
